key_insight: Scaling ego-centric video to 30,000 hours does improve world-model fidelity, but the gains are uneven: the agent representation improves faster than object-interaction understanding. In short, more video helps, but it does not automatically teach robust, general physical interaction.
problem_solved: The paper asks whether massive ego-centric human video can serve as a practical substitute for physics simulators when building world models, especially for out-of-distribution scenes and interactions.
method: Train/evaluate world models using 30,000 hours of ego-centric video spanning 1,000+ scene types and 14,000 contributors.
Measure performance directly on a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark instead of relying only on downstream proxy metrics.
Compare how scaling data affects two capabilities: agent fidelity and object-interaction fidelity.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this paper clarifies the limits of data scaling for world models and shows where additional data still falls short. It helps researchers choose better evaluation targets and reveals that object dynamics may need new model designs, not just more video.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing ego-centric video data flowing into a world model and then into two evaluation branches: agent fidelity and object-interaction fidelity.
A scaling chart illustrating performance gains as training data increases by 100x, with separate curves for agent and interaction understanding.
An out-of-distribution benchmark illustration with example unseen scenes and interaction tasks.
An icon-based comparison of 'what improves' versus 'what remains weak' in the learned world model.
paper_title: What 30,000 Hours of Ego-centric Video Does Not Teach
paper_authors: Jiahua Dong, Anurag Bagchi, Yash Jangir, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov
